name: Quick Sort
description: Divide-and-conquer sort that picks a pivot, partitions elements around it (smaller left, larger right), then recursively sorts partitions. Excellent cache performance makes it fast in practice.
aim: Sort by partitioning: choose a pivot, rearrange so elements ≤ pivot are left and > pivot are right, place pivot in its final position, then recurse on both sides.
howItWorks: Partition: walk with two indices, swap elements out of order
Place pivot at its final sorted position
Base case: size 0 or 1 is sorted

time.bestCase: Pivot always splits array into equal halves
time.averageCase: Random pivot gives expected O(n log n)
time.worstCase: Pivot always smallest or largest (sorted/reverse-sorted input)

complexity.spaceDescription: Recursion stack depth — O(n) in degenerate worst case

realWorld: C stdlib qsort() — most common sort in systems programming
In-memory sort for large random datasets (best cache behavior)
Database query engines for in-memory record sorting
whenToUse: When average-case O(n log n) with good constants is sufficient
In-place sort needed without stability requirement
alternatives: Merge Sort — stable, guaranteed O(n log n), better for linked lists
Heap Sort — in-place guaranteed O(n log n) but worse cache
Randomized Quick Sort — avoids O(n²) worst case in practice
